edges.notes: GPU architecture is an HW/SW-system layer bridge from chip capability to programmer-visible execution.
SIMT is the execution model visible to CUDA programmers.
GPU performance depends heavily on data movement and locality.
Thread/block mapping controls exposed parallelism and scheduler utilization.
Roofline links arithmetic intensity to memory bandwidth and compute ceilings.
Roofline is a first performance model for GPU workloads.
Tensor Cores are specialized matrix units inside modern NVIDIA GPU architectures.
Tensor Core peak throughput is useful only when data movement, precision, and utilization constraints allow it.
TMA is a Hopper-era mechanism for asynchronous tensor-shaped data movement.
Thread block clusters extend the CUDA hierarchy above individual thread blocks.
TMA exists to improve movement through global and shared memory levels.
Clusters are an extension of the existing thread block hierarchy and scheduling model.
The Hopper article presents clusters as a way to coordinate asynchronous units including TMA.
TMA should improve effective bandwidth and overlap only when the workload exposes enough reuse and scheduling structure.
The accelerator ontology is the central map for organizing AI hardware and software concepts.
GPU architecture is one case branch under the accelerator ontology, not the root ontology.
Cerebras WSE tests non-GPU placement through scale-up architecture.
Scaling strategy is a central organizing axis for AI systems.
Software control needs explicit DSL, compiler, runtime, and workload mapping separation.
WSE is modeled as a scale-up strategy case study.
Wafer-scale systems depend on compiler/runtime mapping to make the spatial fabric usable.
Cerebras and GPU systems make different locality and memory movement tradeoffs.
Hardware mechanisms such as TMA become useful through programming, compiler, and runtime exposure.
Scaling decisions often turn on local memory capacity, bandwidth, and communication boundaries.
RVV is a compute substrate mechanism under the accelerator ontology, alongside GPU SIMT and Tensor Cores.
Both provide data-parallel execution; RVV uses explicit vector model while SIMT uses implicit threading. RVV can also serve as substrate for SIMT (Ventus GPGPU).
RVV is a general vector substrate; Tensor Cores are specialized matrix units. The RISC-V Matrix Extension (AME/IME) would be the direct competitor if ratified.
GPU architecture provides contrast for VLA vs. SIMT vs. fixed-width SIMD design philosophy.
Roofline analysis determines whether RVV vectorization benefits are compute-bound or memory-bound in AI workloads.

edges.description: RVV 1.0 is the ratified vector foundation; matrix extension proposals build on or extend it
RVV provides the vector register file and VLA infrastructure that IME and VME depend on; AME optionally interfaces with RVV for data movement
RISC-V matrix extensions and NVIDIA Tensor Cores are competing approaches to matrix multiply acceleration for AI/ML workloads
Matrix extension proposals are a concept within the AI accelerator ontology as a specialized compute substrate pattern
The roofline model measures whether matrix extension benefits are bottlenecked by compute density or memory bandwidth
RISC-V matrix extensions and GPU execution are different approaches to AI compute — one integrates into CPU pipeline, the other into dedicated GPU SMs

edges.notes: RVV memory hierarchy is a sub-concept of the RVV 1.0 compute substrate.
RVV AI SoC memory hierarchy (CPU-like cache + DMA + scratchpad) vs. GPU memory hierarchy (HBM + shared memory + warp scheduling).
RVV vector loads/DMA vs. GPU TMA for asynchronous data staging.
Matrix extensions will impose 2D tile data movement on the memory hierarchy.
Roofline measures memory-bound vs. compute-bound for RVV AI SoCs.
Memory pattern node under the AI accelerator ontology.
RVV 1.0 compute substrate decomposes into compiler auto-vectorization quality as a sub-concept.
Compiler auto-vectorization quality analysis depends on the DSL/compiler/runtime separation framework.
RVV compiler maturity affects feasibility and adoption timeline for matrix extensions.
Auto-vectorization quality is evaluated by how close generated code approaches the roofline ceiling.
VLA compiler auto-vectorization quality competes with fixed-function tensor core programming maturity.
Contrast between VLA auto-vectorization compiler challenges and SIMT compiler maturity.
Auto-vectorization code quality depends on memory hierarchy characteristics.
The AI accelerator ontology decomposes into compiler quality as a key dimension.
RVV 1.0 compute substrate decomposes into AI kernel mapping patterns.
Kernel mapping depends on memory hierarchy for tile sizing and bound determination.
Kernel quality depends on compiler auto-vec or TVM auto-tuning capabilities.
RVV vector GEMM vs GPU Tensor Core matrix multiply.
RVV explicit vector vs GPU SIMT warp-level patterns.
Roofline measures compute-bound vs memory-bound for RVV kernels.
Matrix extensions may supersede RVV GEMM micro-kernel design.
RVV kernel patterns compared with CUDA across memory hierarchy tradeoffs.
Accelerator ontology decomposes into RVV workload mapping as a kernel_algorithm instance.
DSL/compiler/runtime stack enables kernel fusion and auto-tuning for RVV.
